skills.name: British indirect rule in Northern Nigeria

note.text: Indirect rule used selected local rulers and institutions as part of colonial administration under British supervision. Lugard is closely associated with its Northern Nigerian model. Existing emirate structures, limited European personnel, cost concerns and a wish to govern through established authority contributed to its adoption. Rulers did not remain fully sovereign: colonial officials could direct policy and alter or remove office holders. The policy changed local institutions as well as using them, and outcomes varied when applied elsewhere.

sections.heading: Understand the ideas
sections.text: Indirect rule used selected local rulers and institutions as part of colonial administration under British supervision. Lugard is closely associated with its Northern Nigerian model. Existing emirate structures, limited European personnel, cost concerns and a wish to govern through established authority contributed to its adoption. Rulers did not remain fully sovereign: colonial officials could direct policy and alter or remove office holders. The policy changed local institutions as well as using them, and outcomes varied when applied elsewhere.

sections.heading: Apply the ideas locally
sections.text: A resident could supervise an emir whose courts, officials and revenue institutions became part of the colonial framework. The appearance of local continuity did not make the arrangement independent of Britain. A later attempt to use the model in a different society might produce different difficulties; Northern Nigeria should not be assumed identical to every African region.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Explain both the local machinery and the superior colonial authority. Distinguish an official justification from evidence of how the system worked. Assess cost and administrative convenience alongside coercion and changes to local power. Indirect is a method of colonial rule, not the absence of colonial rule.
